summary:
Backscatter is an interactive Earth-observation platform developed by Team Afterimage for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It uses NASA–ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data to investigate changes on Earth's surface, even in cloudy conditions.

Focusing on Kuttanad, Kerala, a region vulnerable to flooding and waterlogging, we developed a web application that compares satellite observations from different dates. Users can explore radar backscatter changes, switch between polarization layers, and inspect individual locations. We also integrated NASA's OPERA surface-water products to provide independent supporting evidence and highlight uncertainties.

Backscatter addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by turning complex satellite measurements into accessible, interactive visualizations that help users investigate environmental changes.

This matters because timely information about changing water conditions can support research, environmental monitoring, and disaster preparedness. Rather than making unsupported flood predictions, Backscatter emphasizes transparent, evidence-based interpretation of real satellite observations.
details:
Backscatter

Backscatter, developed by Team Afterimage, is an interactive satellite radar analysis platform that helps users investigate changes on Earth's surface using real NASA–ISRO NISAR data. Our project focuses on Kuttanad, Kerala, a low-lying region vulnerable to flooding and waterlogging.

How does it work?

Backscatter compares Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations captured on different dates to identify changes in radar backscatter. Unlike conventional optical imagery, SAR can observe Earth's surface even through clouds and without sunlight.

We developed an interactive web application where users can explore before-and-after satellite observations, visualize changes, switch between HH and HV radar polarization layers, and click individual locations to examine actual measurements. We also compare our results against NASA's OPERA surface-water products to provide supporting evidence and assess reliability.

Tools and technologies

Our project was developed using:

  • Frontend: React, JavaScript, MapLibre GL JS, Vite, HTML and CSS.
  • Data processing: Python, NumPy, Rasterio, GDAL and Matplotlib.
  • Satellite data: NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band SAR and NASA OPERA surface-water datasets.
  • Data services: NASA Earthdata, ASF, NASA Harmony and Common Metadata Repository (CMR).
  • Development: Git, GitHub and an Apple Silicon Mac for processing and testing.

Creativity and innovation

Backscatter goes beyond simply displaying satellite imagery. It combines real radar measurements, multiple polarization channels, interactive visualization and independent reference data in one accessible interface.

A key aspect of our approach is scientific transparency. Our experiments demonstrated strong agreement between NISAR measurements and OPERA classifications for existing open water. However, detecting newly flooded or receding areas proved significantly harder. Rather than hiding these limitations, our platform distinguishes measured radar changes from interpretations that require further validation.

Benefits and intended impact

Backscatter makes complex satellite observations easier to understand for students, researchers, environmental organizations and disaster-management teams. It can help users investigate changing water conditions, explore environmental patterns and identify areas that deserve closer examination.

Our goal is to make satellite-based environmental monitoring more accessible, reproducible and trustworthy, particularly for regions affected by seasonal flooding.

Factors we considered

During development, we prioritized data authenticity, scientific reliability, geographical relevance, processing efficiency and ease of use. We also considered cloud cover, differences in satellite acquisition dates, radar calibration, agricultural land-use changes and uncertainty in water classification.

Ultimately, Backscatter transforms complex SAR data into an interactive, evidence-driven experience that helps people understand how Earth's surface is changing—without presenting uncertain interpretations as established facts.
